note: Second-pass CRE Set 3 items. Not copied from Set 2. Each display equation is on its own line.

questions.stem:
Four identical units are independent. The function works if at least three of the four work. Each unit has mission reliability \(R\).
\[
R_{3/4}=4R^{3}(1-R)+R^{4}
\]
What is the mission reliability of the function?
questions.why: At least three means exactly three, plus all four. \[ 4(0.90)^{3}(0.10)=0.2916 \] \[ (0.90)^{4}=0.6561 \] \[ R_{3/4}=0.2916+0.6561=0.9477 \] 0.2916 stops at exactly three. 0.6561 requires all four. 0.9000 is one unit. D. 0.9477

traps.C: Uses the reliability of one unit.

chart.title: Three-out-of-four function
chart.altText: Four identical independent units each have mission reliability 0.90. The function requires at least three of the four.

questions.stem:
Two load blocks are applied in sequence. \(n\) is the cycles applied and \(N\) is the cycles to the failure criterion at that stress. Damage adds by Miner's rule.
\[
D=n_1/N_1+n_2/N_2
\]
What is the cumulative damage?
questions.why: Use each block's own life in its denominator. \[ \frac{2000}{10000}=0.20 \] \[ \frac{1000}{4000}=0.25 \] \[ D=0.20+0.25=0.45 \] 0.20 and 0.25 are single blocks. 0.60 swaps the two lives. The total is below 1, so the rule does not yet predict failure. C. 0.45

traps.D: Pairs each applied-cycle count with the other block's life.

chart.title: Miner load blocks
chart.altText: Block 1 applies 2,000 cycles where the life is 10,000 cycles. Block 2 applies 1,000 cycles where the life is 4,000 cycles.

questions.stem:
Operational availability includes mean logistics delay. Mean time between failures is \(MTBF\), mean repair time is \(MTTR\), and mean logistics delay is \(MLD\).
\[
A_o=\frac{MTBF}{MTBF+MTTR+MLD}
\]
What is the operational availability?
questions.why: Logistics delay is in the denominator for operational availability. Leave it out only for inherent availability. \[ A_o=\frac{700}{800}=0.875 \] 0.100 is logistics delay divided by MTBF. 0.959 removes the logistics delay. 23.3 divides MTBF by the repair time. B. 0.875

chart.title: Operational availability inputs
chart.altText: MTBF is 700 hours, MTTR is 30 hours, and mean logistics delay is 70 hours.

questions.stem:
Three corrective tasks have the shares and durations below. The mean corrective time weights each duration by its share.
\[
MTTR=p_1 t_1+p_2 t_2+p_3 t_3
\]
What is the mean corrective time?
questions.why: Weight the durations. Do not average them as if each task were equally common. \[ MTTR=0.50(20)+0.30(40)+0.20(90) \] \[ MTTR=10+12+18=40 \] 20 minutes is the shortest task. 50 minutes is the unweighted average. 90 minutes is the longest task. B. 40 minutes

traps.A: Uses the most common duration without weighting the others.

chart.title: Corrective-task mix
chart.altText: Half of the tasks take 20 minutes, 30 percent take 40 minutes, and 20 percent take 90 minutes.

questions.stem:
Failures in a month follow a Poisson distribution with mean 3. Use \(e^{-3}=0.0498\).
\[
P(X\le 1)=e^{-3}(1+3)
\]
What is the probability of at most one failure?
questions.why: At most one includes zero and exactly one. \[ P(X\le 1)=0.0498(4)=0.1992 \] 0.0498 is the probability of zero. 0.1494 is the probability of exactly one. 0.9502 is the probability of at least one. C. 0.1992

chart.title: Monthly failure count
chart.altText: The Poisson mean is 3 failures per month. The question asks for the probability of 0 or 1 failure.

questions.stem:
Three independent exponential elements are in series. The mission length is \(t\). Use \(e^{-0.8}=0.4493\).
\[
R(t)=\exp(-\lambda_s t)
\]
\[
\lambda_s=\lambda_1+\lambda_2+\lambda_3
\]
What is the mission reliability?
questions.why: Add the rates, multiply by the mission time, and then take the exponential. \[ \lambda_s=0.001+0.002+0.001=0.004 \] \[ \lambda_s t=0.004(200)=0.8 \] \[ R(200)=e^{-0.8}=0.4493 \] 0.8187 is \(e^{-0.2}\), the reliability of the 0.001 rate alone. 0.9960 is \(e^{-0.004}\), which drops the mission time. 250 hours is the system MTTF, not the reliability. A. 0.4493

traps.B: Uses only one of the small failure rates.
traps.D: Reports the mean life instead of the reliability.

chart.title: Series exponential mission
chart.altText: Element failure rates are 0.001, 0.002, and 0.001 per hour. The mission is 200 hours. The elements are in series and independent.

questions.stem:
The worksheet ranks open actions by the product below. Severity, occurrence, and detection are the table ratings.
\[
RPN=S\times O\times D
\]
Which mode is first under that rule?
options: Modes A and C, because both products equal 120
questions.why: Multiply each row. The largest product is first. Severity does not override a smaller product. \[ RPN_A=8\times 3\times 4=96 \] \[ RPN_B=4\times 8\times 5=160 \] \[ RPN_C=10\times 2\times 6=120 \] Mode C has the highest severity and a product of 120. Mode B has the highest product. B. Mode B

traps.D: Invents a tie that the products do not have.

chart.title: Open FMEA ratings
chart.altText: Mode A has severity 8, occurrence 3, and detection 4. Mode B has severity 4, occurrence 8, and detection 5. Mode C has severity 10, occurrence 2, and detection 6. Rank by the product of the three ratings.

questions.stem:
Three independent dimensions stack. The statistical half-width is the root-sum-square of the half-widths \(t_1\), \(t_2\), and \(t_3\).
\[
t=\sqrt{t_1^{2}+t_2^{2}+t_3^{2}}
\]
What is that half-width?
questions.why: Square, add, and take the square root. Do not add the half-widths. \[ t=\sqrt{0.10^{2}+0.20^{2}+0.20^{2}} \] \[ t=\sqrt{0.09}=0.30 \] ±0.20 is the largest single half-width. ±0.50 is the worst-case sum. ±0.90 squares and adds but does not take the root. B. ±0.30

traps.D: Stops at the sum of the squares.

chart.title: Dimension half-widths
chart.altText: Three independent dimensions have half-widths 0.10, 0.20, and 0.20. The stack uses the root-sum-square.

questions.stem:
Life is lognormal. \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) are the mean and standard deviation of the natural log of life. The 10 percent point of the standard normal distribution is \(z=-1.28\). Use \(e^{4.36}=78.26\), \(e^{3.72}=41.26\), and \(e^{5}=148.41\).
\[
t_{0.10}=\exp(\mu+z\sigma)
\]
What is the B10 life?
questions.why: Multiply \(z\) by \(\sigma\) before adding it to \(\mu\). \[ \mu+z\sigma=5+(-1.28)(0.50)=4.36 \] \[ t_{0.10}=e^{4.36}=78.26 \] 41.26 hours uses \(e^{\mu+z}\) and drops \(\sigma\). 4.36 hours is the log-life. 148.41 hours is the median, \(e^{\mu}\). B. 78.26 hours

traps.A: Adds z to mu and ignores sigma.
traps.C: Stops at the log of life.

chart.title: Lognormal B10 inputs
chart.altText: mu is 5 and sigma is 0.50 on the natural-log scale. The standard-normal value for a 10 percent lower tail is -1.28.

questions.stem:
A fleet of identical units fails at a constant rate \(\lambda\). The fleet size is \(n\) and the exposure of each unit is \(t\).
\[
E=n\lambda t
\]
How many failures are expected?
questions.why: Multiply the fleet size, the rate, and the exposure per unit. \[ E=50(0.002)(1000)=100 \] 2 is \(\lambda t\) for one unit. 50 is the fleet size. 1,000 is the exposure of one unit. C. 100

traps.A: Uses one unit and drops the fleet size.
traps.D: Reports the hours on one unit.

chart.title: Fleet exposure
chart.altText: There are 50 units. Each has failure rate 0.002 per hour and is exposed for 1,000 hours.
